I.
NATURE
OF
APPLICATION

[
1
]

This is an application by most of the named
defendants, to strike the plaintiffs’ claims against them pursuant to
Rules
19(24)
and
57
of the
Supreme Court Rules
, B.C. Reg. 221/90 (“the Rules”).
The application also requires that I address claims made by the plaintiffs
against those defendants who have not entered appearances.

II.
BACKGROUND

[
2
]

The plaintiffs’ statement of claim as amended
prior to the commencement of this hearing consists of 47 single spaced pages
and in excess of 250 paragraphs of allegations and claims against the
defendants.

[
3
]

At its heart, the statement of claim is a
complaint by the plaintiffs against most, if not all, of the governmental
agencies and also those individuals who have not supported; agreed with; or,
lent assistance to the positions and arguments advanced by the plaintiff, L.H.
(formerly L.T.) in her dispute with the defendant, A.T. over the custody of and
access to their infant daughter S.T.

[
4
]

That custody dispute was and is the subject of
the proceedings in this Court in
A.T. v. L.T.T.
, (Vancouver
Registry No. D110334) (the “Custody Action”), in which Madam Justice Morrison
presided over various interlocutory proceedings, a lengthy trial and subsequent
variation applications.

[
5
]

Due to the nature and genesis of the allegations
in the plaintiffs’ statement of claim, it is necessary to review in some
detail: the history of the marital relationship between Ms. L.H. and Mr. A.T.;
some of the history of the Custody Action; other legal proceedings in this
Court and in the courts of South Africa; and, the roles of the various
defendants in some or all of the custody dispute; the related legal
proceedings; and the Custody Action.

A.
History of the Custody Action

[
6
]

Mr. A.T. and Ms. L.H. met on January 15, 1989,
were married on June 17, 1989 in South Africa and then moved to Italy where
their only child, S.T., was born on […], 1996.  In 1997, the family came to
Canada but Mr. A.T. and Ms. L.H. then separated on July 19, 1998.  Their
disputes over the custody of S.T. have been ongoing since that time.

[
7
]

In November of 1998, Martinson J. made an order
in the Custody Action allowing Mr. A.T. interim access to S.T. but made no
custody or guardianship order.

[
8
]

On July 7, 1999, Ms. L.H. and Mr. A.T. entered
into a consent order in the Custody Action that provided for joint guardianship
of S.T.., with Ms. L.S. having sole custody and Mr. A.T. having
generous access.  That consent order also provided that neither parent was to
remove S.T. from British Columbia without the consent of the other.

[
9
]

On May 31, 2000, Ms. L.H. and Mr. A.T. were
divorced and on June 6, 2000, Ms. L.H. advised Mr. A.T. that she wanted to
take S.T. to South Africa to visit her family for one month.

[
10
]

Mr. A.T. then became concerned that Ms. L.H. would not return to
Canada with S.T. and applied for an order to restrain her from taking S.T. to
South Africa.  On that application Mr. A.T. was represented by the
defendant, Jeremy Sheppard and Ms. L.H. was represented by the defendant,
Stanley Schwartz.

[
11
]

On June 9, 2000, Ms. L.H. and Mr. A.T. agreed to a consent order
that granted Ms. L.H. permission to take S.T. to South Africa for a period of
one month but also required that Ms. L.H. deposit a $5,000 bond and provided that
the sole custody of S.T. would revert to Mr. A.T. in the event Ms. L.H. did
not return to British Columbia by July 14, 2000.  That consent order also
provided for: a s. 15 assessment under the

Family Relations Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128; the expeditious setting of a trial date; and, that Mr.
A.T. would have telephone access to S.T. in South Africa, as well as extended
summer access upon S.T.’s return to Canada.

[
12
]

On June 12, 2000, Ms. L.H. and S.T. travelled to South Africa but on
July 14, 2000, Ms. L.H.’s father telephoned Mr. A.T. to tell him that Ms.
L.H. and S.T. would not be returning to Canada.

[
13
]

Mr. A.T. then applied to this Court for an order confirming sole
custody and guardianship pursuant to the provisions of the consent order made on
June 9, 2000.  On July 21, 2000, Holmes J. granted that order and also ordered
that Ms. L.H. immediately deliver S.T. to Mr. A.T.’s custody.

[
14
]

Mr. A.T. also went to the police for assistance in compelling Ms.
L.H. to return S.T. to Canada and charges were eventually laid by the police
against Ms. L.H. as well as Mr. V.H. under the provisions of
s. 283
of the

Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 concerning S.T.’s alleged abduction.

[
15
]

Subsequent to the order of Holmes J., both Ms. L.H. and Mr. A.T.
brought applications concerning custody of S.T. in the High Court of South
Africa and on October 16, 2000, that court ordered that S.T. be returned to
Canada.  Ms. L.H. then appealed that order.

[
16
]

On November 23, 2000, the Constitutional Court of South Africa
confirmed Mr. A.T.’s custody of S.T. and also ordered that she was to be
returned to Canada under certain conditions.  One of those conditions was that Ms.
L.H. would not be arrested upon her return to Canada.

[
17
]

Although there was considerable delay in the implementation of the
order of the Constitutional Court of South Africa, on March 30, 2001, pursuant
to a further application by Mr. A.T. in the Custody Action, Morrison J. ordered
that S.T. be returned to Mr. A.T.’s custody in British Columbia upon the same
terms and conditions as those imposed by the Constitutional Court of South
Africa, including the condition that Ms. L.H. would not be arrested upon her
return to Canada.

[
18
]

After making her order of March 30, 2001, Morrison J. became seized
of all matters related to the custody of and access to S.T. until mid 2004 as I
shall later discuss.

[
19
]

On June 14, 2001, Ms. L.H. finally returned to Canada with S.T.
after an absence of almost one full year.  Although she was not arrested upon
her return, the police did meet her and ask her to attend at their offices.  Ms.
L.H. eventually complied with that request and was charged with the abduction
of S.T.  It is those actions by the police and the subsequent prosecution of
those and other criminal charges against both Ms. L.H. and Mr. V.H. related to
other breaches of the orders of this Court in the Custody Action that form the
basis of the plaintiffs’ allegations against the defendant, the Crown Counsel
of British Columbia and, in part, against the defendant, the Legal Services
Society.

[
20
]

In July, 2001, the defendant, Stanley Schwartz, ceased to act for Ms. L.H.
and in that same month Ms. L.H. married her present husband, the plaintiff, V.H..

[
21
]

Various access problems arose after Ms. L.H.’s return to Canada
which resulted in many orders being made by Morrison J. in the Custody
Action.

[
22
]

Those orders included the appointment of the defendant, Michelle
Fuchs, as a child advocate for S.T. and the ordering of a s. 15 custody and
access report under the
Family Relations Act

that was eventually
completed by the defendant, Dr. Paul Eirikson on December 10, 2001
.

[
23
]

The trial in the Custody Action commenced on January 29, 2002 and
consisted of 28 days of evidence and submissions heard by Morrison J.
intermittently over four months, ending on May 22, 2002.

[
24
]

During the trial Mr. A.T. was represented by the defendant, Ian
Hayward, while Ms. L.H. acted on her own behalf and the defendant, Michelle
Fuchs, represented S.T.

[
25
]

Dr. Eirikson’s s. 15 report was filed with the Court and he also
testified at the trial.

[
26
]

Other witnesses at the trial who are now named as defendants in this
proceeding were: the defendant, Susan Henry, who was then a close friend of Ms.
L.H.; the defendant, Cathy Ratz, S.T.’s kindergarten teacher; the defendant,
Paul Lorette, the principal of the school now attended by S.T. but who, at the
time he gave evidence, had never met S.T. or her parents; and, the defendant, J.
(J.) O., who was Ms. L.H.’s step-cousin and who eventually, together with her
husband, the defendant, P.O. became a supervisor of some of Mr. A.T.’s access
visits with S.T.

[
27
]

On June 28, 2002, Morrison J. delivered her reasons for judgment in
the Custody Action under
A.T. v. L.T.T
.,
2002 BCSC 981
.  Morrison
J. ordered, among other things, that: Mr. A.T. and Ms. L.H. would share
joint custody and guardianship of S.T.; S.T.’s primary residence would be with
Ms. L.H. except for most of the summer months and during certain vacation
times; neither party would remove S.T. from Canada except by agreement or
further court order; each party would surrender any passport that they held for
S.T.; neither party would deny access of the other to S.T. unless she was ill,
in which case that lost access would be made up within the next two months; Mr.
A.T. would have specified access to S.T. during the school year consisting of
every second weekend and one afternoon and evening mid-week; and, that Mr. A.T.
would also have additional weekend access during holiday and school break
periods.  Morrison J. further ordered Mr. A.T. and Ms. L.H. to take part
in post-marital counselling for a minimum of six sessions each and that the
parties were to communicate directly with one another rather than through Mr.
A.T.’s lawyer.

[
28
]

A synopsis of Morrison J.’s reasons for judgment was published by
the defendant, the Continuing Legal Education Society.  As will be later
discussed,

Ms. L.H. alleges that the synopsis is defamatory.

[
29
]

After the trial in the Custody Action, custody and access problems
continued.

[
30
]

Mr. and Ms. L.H. continued to make allegations, as Ms. L.H. had
since 1998, in this Court and in the courts of South Africa, that Mr. A.T. had
been and was still physically and sexually abusing S.T. and was negligent in
his care of her when exercising access.

[
31
]

Notwithstanding that Morrison J. had determined that there was no
substance to all of the allegations that had been made both up to and during
the trial, the plaintiffs continued to insist that S.T. was constantly making
new “disclosures” to Ms. L.H..  The plaintiffs reported most, if not all, of
these new allegations to: some or all of the defendants, the West Vancouver
Police Department; the RCMP; the Ministry of Children and Family Development;
and, others.  They also from time to time refused or hindered Mr. A.T.’s access
to S.T. because of these new disclosures notwithstanding Morrison J.’s orders
and directions to the contrary.

[
32
]

Specifically, on March 11, 2003, Ms. L.H. made further allegations
of sexual abuse against Mr. A.T. and denied his access to S.T.  As a
consequence of the allegations made by the plaintiffs, Morrison J. made an
interim order for supervised access to S.T. by Mr. A.T. pending further
investigation and a full hearing.  In making that order Morrison J. determined
that, in her view, the defendants, Susan Henry and J.O., both of whom had
testified at the original trial, would be appropriate supervisors of access by
Mr. A.T. to S.T. pending the full hearing of Ms. L.H.’s new allegations of
sexual impropriety against Mr. A.T..

[
33
]

The plaintiffs’ new allegations against Mr. A.T. and their denial of
access as ordered by Morrison J. not only gave rise to Morrison J.’s supervised
access order pending the full hearing of those allegations, but also gave rise
to further police investigation of the circumstances that eventually resulted
in the police bringing further
Criminal Code

charges against both
Mr. V.H. and Ms. L.H. for their unilateral actions in defiance of Morrison J.’s
orders.

[
34
]

On July 17, 2003, Morrison J. considered all of the new allegations
made against Mr. A.T. by the plaintiffs and again determined that there was no
substance to the allegations.  In that hearing, Morrison J. considered affidavits
that were sworn by the defendants, Heather Bradner and Anita Jaegar, as well as
an updated s. 15 custody and access report prepared by Dr. Eirikson that
recommended that S.T.’s primary residence be with Mr. A.T. rather than Ms. L.H..

[
35
]

In oral reasons in the Custody Action filed on July 17, 2003, Morrison
J. accepted Dr. Eirikson’s recommendations and ordered a change in S.T.’s
principal residence.  She also ordered that Mr. A.T. would be entrusted with
the sole custody of S.T. although her guardianship would remain joint.  In
addition, Morrison J. made specific orders concerning Ms. L.H.’s access to
S.T. and terminated the order that had required Mr. A.T. to pay child
support to Ms. L.H..

[
36
]

Ms. L.H. did not willingly accept Morrison J.’s order of July 17,
2003, and after virtually every access visit by S.T., made further allegations
of S.T.’s continued new disclosures of physical and sexual abuse by Mr. A.T.
which she again reported to some or all of the defendants, the Ministry of
Children and Family Development, the RCMP and the West Vancouver Police
Department.

[
37
]

After a further year of turmoil concerning the custody of and access
to S.T. and a further series of continuing and unabated complaints by the
plaintiffs about Mr. A.T.’s alleged misconduct towards S.T., on July 5, 2004,
Mr. A.T. brought an application in the Custody Action before Morrison J.
seeking, among other things, that Ms. L.H.’s access to S.T. be supervised.
In response, Ms. L.H. brought counter-applications seeking, among other
things, sole custody of S.T. and further investigation of S.T. as well as of
Mr. A.T.’s conduct toward S.T.

[
38
]

During the hearing of those applications in July 2004, Ms. L.H.
requested that Morrison J. not remain seized of the issues in the Custody
Action and Morrison J agreed.  That decision resulted in the adjournment of the
hearing of the July, 2004 variation applications to November, 2004 and the appointment
of a new judge in the Custody Action.

[
39
]

Those variation applications were heard by me over a number of days
from mid-November, 2004 to mid-January, 2005 and I have reserved judgment.

B.
The Related Criminal Proceedings

[
40
]

As I have noted above, in July 2001, Mr. and Ms. L.H. were charged
with abduction under the
Criminal Code

and in March 2003, they
were also charged under the provisions of
s. 129
of the
Criminal
Code
with breaching Morrison J.’s access orders.

[
41
]

Ms. L.H. was committed to stand trial on the abduction charges after
a preliminary hearing in February 2002, but thereafter applied for a stay of those
charges alleging an abuse of process by the Crown in having charged her with
abduction in the face of Morrison J.’s order in the Custody Action that Ms.
L.H. would not be arrested upon her return to Canada.  In addition to that stay
application, Ms. L.H. also applied for the appointment of counsel on her behalf
in the abduction proceedings or, in the alternative, a stay of those
proceedings pending the appointment of counsel.  Those applications arose as a
consequence of the refusal by the defendant, the Legal Aid Society, to appoint
counsel for Ms. L.H. because it had determined that she had failed to establish
that she met the applicable financial criteria.

[
42
]

Eventually, after considerable delay in the prosecution of the
abduction charges, they were joined for trial with the charges concerning the
alleged breaches of Morrison J.’s custody and access orders.  The trial of all
charges was then set to be heard in this Court in late 2004.

[
43
]

In July 2004, however, after further numerous pre-trial proceedings
in relation to all of the criminal charges, Ms. L.H. entered a plea of
guilty to the alleged breaches of this Court’s orders and, in return, the Crown
agreed to stay proceedings against Ms. L.H. in relation to the original
abduction charge, as well as against Mr. V.H. in relation to all charges.  The criminal
matters were then set over to a sentencing hearing to be conducted in October
2004.

[
44
]

On October 22, 2004, after a three day sentencing hearing before
Melnick J., Ms. L.H. was sentenced to a Conditional Sentence totalling four
months in duration as well as to a period of probation for her breaches of the
court orders.

C.
This
and other Related Civil Proceedings

[
45
]

On March 1, 2004, the plaintiffs commenced this proceeding against
all of the named defendants except Sergeant Barber and Detective Kravjansky of
the West Vancouver Police Department and Constables Jordan Dupuis and Paul
Sellers of the RCMP.

[
46
]

On September 1, 2004, the plaintiffs filed a petition in the
Vancouver Registry of this Court under file number L042195 (the “Judicial
Review Petition”).  In the Judicial Review Petition the plaintiffs not only
sought to have all of Morrison J.’s orders in the Custody Action reviewed and
overturned, but also sought declaratory relief against many of the defendants
in this proceeding for their alleged wrongdoing in the Custody Action
concerning most if not all of the issues that are also the subject of this
proceeding.

[
47
]

On October 6, 2004, the Judicial Review Petition was dismissed in
its entirety by Melnick J. as an abuse of process under
Rule 19(24)
(d)
.

[
48
]

After a joint Case Management Conference in this proceeding and in
the Custody Action held before me on November 15, 2004, I determined that I
would proceed with the hearing of the applications by the defendants in this
proceeding and also with the hearing of the variation applications in the
Custody Action as soon as time became available for both cases.

[
49
]

Immediately after that Case Management Conference the plaintiffs
filed an amended statement of claim in this proceeding under Rule 24(1)(a) that
significantly expanded upon their claims against some of the defendants.  That amendment
also purported to add S.T. as a plaintiff and Sergeant Barber and Detective
Kravjansky of the West Vancouver Police Department and Constables Jordan Dupuis
and Paul Sellers of the RCMP as defendants.  In addition, it purported to
delete the West Vancouver Police Department as a named defendant.

[
50
]

As a consequence of the filing of the plaintiffs’ amended statement
of claim, before commencing the hearing the defendants’ applications under
Rule

19(24)
to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims, I ordered that:

(1)  the purported joinder of S.T. as a plaintiff was of no
effect since her involvement as an infant plaintiff was not properly authorized
and no
guardian ad litem
had been appointed.  I also ordered that on the
present
Rule 19(24)
applications I would not consider any possible actions that
S.T. might be able to maintain against any of the defendants who have allegedly
caused her harm and that any such allegations would be considered only with
leave of the Court after service upon both Mr. A.T. and any allegedly effected
defendants. I further ordered that I will be seized of any such applications
unless I otherwise order;

(2)  the purported joinder of Sergeant Barber and Detective
Kravjansky of the West Vancouver Police Department and Constables Jordan Dupuis
and Paul Sellers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (the “RCMP”) as
defendants is of no effect and also ordered that the plaintiffs may not commence
any proceedings against those or any other defendants that are not presently
named in this proceeding without leave of the Court after personal service upon
any such proposed defendants and that I will be seized of any such applications
unless I otherwise order; and

(3)  the defendants’ applications under Rule 19(24) would be
determined on the basis of the pleadings in the amended statement of claim
except in relation to the claims purportedly advanced on behalf of S.T. and
against the individual police officers who had not been properly joined as
defendants.

[
51
]

On November 23, 2004, after hearing the submissions of all parties
in relation to the defendants’ applications under
Rule

19(24)
in this
proceeding, I provided some preliminary oral reasons for judgment with written
reasons to follow.

[
52
]

These are those written reasons.  To the extent that I may have
reached any different conclusions than initially indicated in my oral reasons,
these reasons and the orders now made will govern the disposition of all of the
defendants’ applications and the further conduct of this proceeding.

III.
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION

[
53
]

Rule

19(24) provides that:

At any stage of a proceeding the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no reasonable claim or defence
as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious,

(c) it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the process of
the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order the
proceedings to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[
54
]

The defendants have submitted that the pleadings are scandalous,
unnecessary and vexatious, and that to permit this action to proceed would
involve unnecessary and unjustifiable expense.  The defendants have further
submitted that the plaintiffs are attempting to re-litigate the issues that
were decided in the Custody Action such that these proceedings amount to a
collateral attack on the decisions of this Court in the Custody Action and in the
related criminal proceedings, and as such are an abuse of process.

[
55
]

To succeed on an application under
Rule 19(24)
, the defendant must
show that it is “plain and obvious” that the pleadings offend any one of the
subrules in
Rule

19(24)
.

[
56
]

A useful summary of the criteria to be applied in determining
whether pleadings should be struck under the various subsections of Rule 19(24)
is found in
Wayneroy Holdings Ltd. v. British Columbia (Minister of
Environment, Lands and Parks)
,
2002 BCSC 1510
.

[
57
]

As to the potential application of
Rule 19(24)
(a) to impugned
pleadings, Romilly J. stated at ¶ 12 and 13 that:

Under R. 19(24)(a) of the
Rules of Court

a court may order that the pleadings be struck out in their entirety or in part
because they fail to disclose a reasonable cause of action.  As to what is
required to succeed on a R. 19(24)(a) application, I will quote from my
judgment in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.) at para.
34
:

To succeed on an
application under Rule 19(24)(a) it must be established that it is “plain and
obvious” that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt v.
Carey
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.).  If there is any doubt it should
be resolved in the favour of permitting the pleadings to stand:
McGauley v.
British Columbia
(1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223 (B.C.C.A.).  The court
should proceed on the assumption that all facts pled are true:
Helman v.
Brown
(1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C.C.A.).  The only question then is
whether the facts disclose a cause of action:
Minnes v. Minnes
(1962),

1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.);
McNaughten v. Baker
(1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d)
17 (C.A.).  In other words, as long as the pleadings disclose a triable
issue, either as it exists, or as it may be amended, then the issue should go

no ground for striking it out under the provisions of Rule 19(24):

supra
.

[13]

v. Ensign
,

, [1999] B.C.J. No. 1172 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.) at para.
33

Factors to be considered in the “plain and
obvious” rule include, but are not limited to: (1) whether there is a question
to be tried regardless of complexity or novelty; (2) whether the outcome of the
trial is beyond a reasonable doubt; (3) whether serious questions of law or
questions of general importance are raised or if facts should be known before
rights are decided; (4) whether the pleadings may be amended; and (5) whether
there is an element of abuse of process:
Midwest Management (1987)
Ltd. v. B.C. Gas Utility Ltd.

(1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 186 (B.C.S.C.)
.

[

what constitutes pleadings that are “unnecessary”, “scandalous”, “frivolous”,
or “embarrassing”. However some principles do emerge.

Irrelevancy and embarrassment are both

(1987),

1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.).  An “embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is

(1985),

1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (B.C.C.A.) at 147.

…

advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan

(December 2,

…

B.C. Rail Ltd

judicata
and collateral attack.

[
61

Res judicata
is grounded upon two broad
principles of public policy: first, that the state has an interest that there
should be an end to litigation and, second, that no individual should be sued
more than once for the same cause.  (See:
Angle v. Minister of National Revenue

(1974),
1974 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248 at 267, 47 D.L.R. (3d) 544)

[
62

In
McIntosh v. Parent
(1924),
1924 CanLII 401 (ON SCAD)
, 55 O.L.R. 552 at 555,
[1924] 4 D.L.R. 420 (Ont. C.A.), the Court stated the common law rule of
res
judicata
in these terms:

When a question is
litigated the judgment of the Court is a final determination between the
parties and their privies.  Any right, question or fact distinctly put in issue
and directly determined by a court of competent jurisdiction as a ground of
recovery or as an answer to a claim set up cannot be retried in a subsequent
suit between the same parties or their privies though for a different cause of
action.  The right, question or fact once determined must as between them be taken
to be conclusively established so long as the judgment remains.

[
63
]

The doctrine of collateral attack was described by McIntyre J. in
R.
v. Wilson,
1983 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594 at 596, 4 D.L.R. (4th) 577:

It has long been a
fundamental rule that a court order made by a court having jurisdiction to make
it, stands and is binding and conclusive unless it is set aside on appeal or
lawfully quashed.  It is also well settled in the authorities that such an
order may not be attacked collaterally - and a collateral attack may be
described as an attack made in proceedings other than those whose specific
object is the reversal, variation, or nullification of the order or judgment.
Where appeals have been exhausted and other means of direct attack upon a
judgment or order, such as proceedings by prerogative writs or proceedings for
judicial review, have been unavailing, the only recourse open to one who seeks
to set aside a court order is an action for review in the High Court where
grounds would include fraud or discovery of new evidence.

[
64
]

Generally and broadly speaking therefore, the doctrines of
res
judicata
and collateral attack

each act as a form of estoppel either
as to the cause of action advanced or the issues that have already been
conclusively decided to prevent unsuccessful litigants from re-arguing points
of fact or law that have already been decided against them in properly
constituted proceedings.

[
65
]

Wedge J. then determined that the action brought
against opposing counsel was an abuse of process that should not be permitted
to continue.

[
111
]

Jensen v. MacGregor
is also applicable in this case. In
Jensen
,
the
plaintiff and his wife separated and his wife retained the defendant solicitors
for legal advice about that separation.  The plaintiff alleged that as a result
of that advice his wife reduced his access to the couple’s children. The
plaintiff asserted that defence counsel owed him a duty of care and had a duty
to act in the best interests of the children.  Defence counsel then applied
under Rule

19(24) for an order striking out the statement of claim.  Madam
Justice Sinclair Prowse granted the application on the basis that a lawyer only
owes a duty to the court and to his or her client.

[
112
]

I see no basis upon which the plaintiffs’
allegations against either or both of Mr. Hayward and Mr. Sheppard are in
any way actionable.  I am also satisfied that the allegations are frivolous,
vexatious and embarrassing and must be struck as an abuse of process.

Fuchs

[
113
]

Action and with the plaintiffs was that she acted in the capacity of a court

[
114
]

must be dismissed on the same basis as their allegations against Mr. Sheppard

[

]

Rules

H.
The Plaintiffs’
Allegations Against the Defendant, Dr. Paul Eirikson

[
116
]

Dr. Paul Eirikson was involved in the Custody
Action only in the capacity of an expert witness appointed under
s. 15
of
the
Family Relations Act
to provide a custody and access report
to assist the Court in the assessment of S.T.’s best custodial and access
interests.

[
117
]

The plaintiffs’ claims against Dr. Eirikson must
be dismissed by reason of the absolute immunity from litigation arising from
witness privilege as well as by reason of the fact that he was a court
appointed expert who provided no therapeutic counselling to S.T. or either of
the plaintiffs.

[
118
]

The defence of absolute privilege operates to
exempt any witness from liability for statements and investigations they make
in the course of judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings.  It is the context in
which the statements are made, rather than the nature of the statements or the witness
making them, which gives rise to the defence.  There are also numerous reported
cases in which the absolute privilege that attaches to any witness has been
extended to the testimony of a professional expert witness engaged in the
course of the legal process.

[
119
]

In
Fabian v. Margulies
,
1985 CanLII 2063 (ON CA)
, [1984]
O.J. No. 1023 (Ont. H.C.), the plaintiff claimed damages for malpractice
against a psychiatrist on the basis that the psychiatrist’s report concerning the
plaintiff in other litigation was wrong. Labrosse J. ruled that a medical legal
opinion given in the context of litigation cannot form the basis of a
malpractice action and dismissed the plaintiff’s action as disclosing no
reasonable cause of action.

[
120
]

In
Kravit v. Dilli
(1998),
1998 CanLII 5180 (BC SC)
, 56
B.C.L.R. (3d) 150 (B.C.S.C.), Madam Justice Baker held that a risk assessment
drafted by a psychiatrist at the request of Crown counsel attracted absolute
privilege in circumstances where the plaintiff alleged that the psychiatrist’s report
was negligently, falsely and maliciously prepared.  In dismissing the plaintiff’s
claims, Baker J. stated at ¶
23
that:

… The privilege
applies whether the evidence of the witness is tendered orally or through the
production of written documents, and extends to testimony submitted in the form
of a letter or report, as well as statements made to counsel or a party to a
lawsuit, in anticipation of giving testimony.

[
121
]

Baker J. also determined that even if the
defence of absolute privilege had not been available to the defendant, his
report would nevertheless be entitled to immunity based on qualified privilege.
She stated at ¶ 34:

In my view, Dr.
Dilli, in the conduct of his profession, had a legitimate interest in assisting
Crown Counsel to assess the risk to persons working in the justice system, and
to others … Having undertaken his assessment and having come to the conclusions
expressed in his report, Dr. Dilli also had a duty to provide his opinion to
Crown Counsel, in order that it be available for use in anticipated criminal
proceedings, or in certification proceedings under the
Mental Health Act
.

[
122
]

The facts of this case establish that Dr.
Eirikson performed no tasks and gave no advice or opinions other than in his
role as a court appointed expert.  It is, in my view, immaterial that he was
nominated for those services by Ms. Fuchs rather than appointed by
Morrison J. of her own motion.  What is in issue is the nature and the purpose
of the tasks undertaken and the expert witness role in which those tasks were
undertaken, not the substance of the opinion or the appointment process.

[
123
]

I am accordingly satisfied that as a consequence
of absolute witness privilege, as well as the privilege arising from Dr.
Eirikson’s appointment as a court appointed expert who was not involved in any
way as a treating psychologist or counsellor for any of the parties in the
Custody Action for S.T., the plaintiffs’ claims against him must be dismissed
as disclosing no reasonable cause of action under Rule 19(24)(a).

I.
The
Plaintiffs’ Allegations Against the Defendants, Cathy Ratz, Susan Henry, Michael
Henry, P.O., J.O., Heather Bradner, Paul Lorette and Anita Jaegar (the “defendant
Witnesses”)

[
124
]

As I have discussed in relation to the
plaintiffs’ claims against Dr. Eirikson, every witness who testifies in  litigation
proceedings is protected from being sued in relation to that testimony by
reason of absolute privilege.

[
125
]

The rationale for the absolute immunity from
suit afforded by the law to witnesses in judicial and quasi-judicial
proceedings that has existed since at least the eighteenth century is that the
immunity exists for the benefit of the public.  The administration of justice
would be greatly impeded if witnesses were to be in fear that any disgruntled
and possibly impecunious person against whom they gave evidence might involve
them in costly litigation and thus the only remedy available against a witness
who gives false evidence is a prosecution for perjury.  (See:
M.A. v.
(Guardian ad Litem of) v. I.A.S.M.A.
(1992),
1992 CanLII 254 (BC CA)
, 69 B.C.L.R. (2d) 99 (B.C.C.A.).

[
126
]

With the exception of the defendant, Mr. Paul
Lorette, and the defendants J.O. and P.O., (against whom the plaintiffs make
some additional allegations that I will later discuss), the allegations against
each of the defendant Witnesses relates solely to their testimony before Morrison
J. at the trial in the Custody Action or to affidavits filed in the variation
proceedings in the Custody Action.  During argument, Ms. L.H. also admitted
that the sole basis of her claims against the defendant Witnesses as witnesses
was that they had committed perjury.

[
127
]

Perjury is a crime; it is not the basis for a
civil cause of action.  As was succinctly stated by Cullen J. in
Hanson
v. Canada (Revenue General)
(1990),
1990 CanLII 13409 (FC)
, 38 F.T.R. 34 (F.C.T.D.) at p. 40:

As no criminal proceedings have been
instituted, the plaintiff is left with a civil action, but there is no civil
action for perjury known to the common law.  As is stated in Clerk
, Clerk
and Lindsell on Torts
(16th Ed. Agincourt, Ont.: Carswell, 1989), at p.
1068:

“
No civil action
for perjury
.  It is said that ‘neither party, witness, counsel, jury or
judge can be put to answer civilly or criminally for words spoken in office’.
Thus there is absolute privilege in an action for defamation and no civil
action lies against a witness for perjury at the suit of the person damnified
by the false evidence.  The immunity is immunity from any form of civil action,
e.g. conspiracy to defame.”

Also, Fleming,
The Law on Torts
, (6th Ed.,
Agincourt, Ont.: Carswell 1983), at p. 580:

“But no civil action
whatever lies for bearing false witness, as distinct from maliciously
maintaining proceedings; the advance of public justice is thought to be best
served by not fettering testimony, aside from the criminal sanction for
perjury.”

[Emphasis
in original]

[
128
]

The plaintiffs’ claims against the defendant
Witnesses that relate in any way to their testimony or their affidavits filed
in the Custody Action are accordingly dismissed under Rule 19(24)(a) as
disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

[
129
]

In addition to their allegations against the
defendant, J.O., as a witness in the Custody Action, the plaintiffs allege that
she and her husband, P.O., caused harm to S.T. while she was under their
supervision and control by reason of the orders of Morrison J. by failing to
ensure that S.T. obtained appropriate dental care.  Those allegations as
advanced by the plaintiffs are dismissed since even if they are of substance,
they are causes of actions that would only be available to S.T.  As such, the
allegations in the amended statement of claim are not now before the Court
since S.T. has not been properly joined as a plaintiff in this proceeding.

[
130
]

In addition to their allegations against the
defendant, Paul Lorette, as a witness, the plaintiffs have also alleged that
Mr. Lorette, as the principal of the school which S.T. was attending after
Morrison J.’s order of July 13, 2003, failed to provide proper supervisory care
for S.T.’s needs so that she suffered frostbite.  Again, to the extent that
they are presently before the Court as claims by the plaintiffs, those
allegations must be dismissed since even if they are of substance they would only
be actionable by S.T. who has not been properly joined as a plaintiff in this
proceeding.  I also take this opportunity to remind the plaintiffs, as I did
both during argument and in my oral reasons, that even if they seek leave to attempt
to pursue any action on behalf of S.T. concerning the matters alleged, such an
action against Mr. Lorette or any other individual administrator or teacher
charged with S.T.’s care, may be precluded by the provisions of
s. 94
of the
School
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 412.

[
131
]

In summary, the plaintiffs’ claims as presently
framed against all of the defendant Witnesses are dismissed under Rule

19(24)(a).

The Plaintiffs’ Allegations Against the Defendant, the
Continuing Legal Education Society

[

The claim against the defendant, the Continuing

The Defendant, the

and amendments thereto, and the
UN
Convention on the Rights of the Child.

the plaintiffs’ allegation against the Continuing Legal Education Society of

trial decision in the Custody Action which stated that:

in 1998.  They had one child, a daughter now aged six.  Despite acrimony
between the parties, they were initially able to agree that the child’s
residence would be with the defendant wife and that the plaintiff husband would

In fact, it was the wife herself who was guilty of abuse
.  On many
occasions, particularly after access visits by the husband, she subjected the

[Emphasis added]

[

Ms. L.H. alleges that the above synopsis and

[

]

Rule 19(12) requires that allegations of
defamation must be pleaded by a plaintiff with particularity and that defences

[
136
]

It would, in my opinion, be inappropriate to
dismiss Ms. L.H.’s allegations of defamation as frivolous before she has an
opportunity to particularize those allegations.

137

I accordingly order that the application of the
defendant, the Continuing Legal Education Society to dismiss the plaintiffs’

Rule

19(24)(a) with respect to Mr.
V.H.’s claims since he has identified no basis upon which such a claim by him

additionally, those allegations must be

Doern v. Phillips Estate
(1994),
1994 CanLII 1869 (BC SC)
, 2 B.C.L.R.
(3d) 349 (B.C.S.C.);
Grassi v. WIC Radio Ltd.
,

2000
BCSC 185
;
Dixon v. Deacon Morgan
(1989),

[1997]
B.C.J. No. 1779 (S.C.) (QL)
; and

L.
The
Plaintiffs’ Allegations Against the Defendant, the Legal Services Society of
British Columbia (the “Legal Services Society”)

[
141
]

The plaintiffs allege that the Legal Services
Society wrongfully failed to provide legal counsel for Ms. L.H. in the
Custody Action and in the early stages of the criminal proceedings and in so
doing breached its obligations to her.

[
142
]

The plaintiffs’ claims against the Legal
Services Society are complicated by the fact that the statutory framework that
governs the provision of legal services to those who qualify for the provision
of such services has changed since 2001 when Ms. L.H. returned to Canada with S.T.
from South Africa and then began to represent herself in the Custody Action and
in the related criminal proceedings.

[
143
]

At that time, and at all material times prior to
May 9, 2002, the Legal Services Society was governed by the provisions of the
Legal
Services Society Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 256, which to the extent
relevant to these proceedings provided in
s. 3
that:

3.(1)  The objects of the society are to ensure
that

(a) services ordinarily provided by a lawyer
are afforded to individuals who would not otherwise receive them because of
financial or other reasons; and

(b) education, advice and information about law
are provided for the people of British Columbia.

(2)  The society shall ensure, for the purposes
of subsection (1)(a), that legal services are available for a qualifying individual
who

(a) is a defendant in criminal proceedings that
could lead to his imprisonment;

(b) may be imprisoned or confined through civil
proceedings;

(c) is or may be a party to a proceedings
respecting a domestic dispute that affects his physical or

mental safety or health or that of his
children; or

(d) has a legal problem that threatens

(i)
his family’s physical or mental safety or health;

(ii) his
ability to feed, clothe and provide shelter for himself and his dependents; or

(iii) his
livelihood.

]

On May 9, 2002, the
Legal Services Society
Act,
S.B.C. 2002, c. 30 received Royal Assent.  Sections 9, 10 and 11
are the sections of the successor
Legal Services Society Act

that
are relevant to the allegations of the plaintiffs for the period following May

Also, the plaintiffs have alleged breaches of

and

the plaintiffs in these submissions in my attempt to understand the nature of

they also remain the subject of the variation proceedings that are presently
being heard by me in the Custody Action.

[
153
]

In all of those circumstances, I am satisfied
that all of the allegations against Mr. A.T. in this proceeding must be struck
as an abuse of process under Rule

19(24)(d). The plaintiffs are estopped
by the doctrines of
res judicata
and collateral attack from attempting
to re-litigate all issues raised concerning events prior to September 1, 2004.
Further, these proceedings are entirely duplicitous with respect to the issues
raised in the Custody Action from and after July 17, 2003, that are being
presently determined by me, and as such are not only unnecessary but also
oppressive, embarrassing and vexatious.
